Basic TUI in a tiny harness - part 6

Up to now, watching a coding agent run inside our harness (the small program wrapped around the model) has meant waiting for it to finish and then opening a log file. Run npm run tui instead and the terminal narrates as it goes: the task, the model choosing to write a file, the request with the path and the two letters ok, the yes, the result, the byte check, and stop. Each line shows up a moment after the matching record lands on disk.

Last time we gave the agent three kinds of memory: scratch for one run, notes that last across steps in the same run, and a durable file that survives a restart. The same name could hold a different value in each, and only the step-to-step note was used to fill hello.txt. Catch up here: Memory kinds in a tiny harness - part 5.

This time we build a basic text user interface (TUI), which here means a plain view made of lines of text in the terminal, with no windows or buttons. The log file stays the source of truth. The screen only reprints each event after it has been written, so the two can never disagree.

You will learn how a single pure function (one that only turns input into output and touches nothing else) can turn any log record into display lines, why writing to disk first and printing second keeps the view honest, how the same renderer replays an old log with no model and no file writes, and how to drop terminal colors cleanly when the output goes to a file.

1424 chars

Starting simple: one log, two surfaces

The small runtime wrapped around the model is the harness. It already writes a log, transcripts/tui.jsonl for this demo. The log is one JavaScript Object Notation object per line, a format people call JSONL. The TUI is a projector. Each journal event (one record in that log) becomes one or more lines on standard output (stdout for short), the stream the terminal shows. The file stays the source. The terminal reprints it.

The scripted guest with no network call is FakeModel. In ok mode it proposes write_file for hello.txt with content ok, then stops once a tool message exists. The harness still asks for Allow before the write. Allow means yes, and the write does not start until that yes is recorded. Tests bake that yes into a helper so continuous integration (the robot that re-runs the suite, usually shortened to CI) never waits on a keyboard. That helper is FixedGate. You pass allow, or deny, or timeout when you create it, and it returns that word at once. Timeout is a third pre-set word so a test can skip the write without anyone watching a clock.

The code is public:

https://github.com/ashishpatill/harness-from-scratch

Clone it and run npm run tui. Watch the terminal, then open transcripts/tui.jsonl. The tags on the screen should match the events in the file. hello.txt still reads ok.

The picture is that match.

The title is Same objects, two surfaces. The left card is JSONL lines: user, model_decision, tool_request, approval, observation, proof, stop. The right card is tagged stdout, captioned terminal reprint: [task], [model], a tool tag, [gate] allow in green, [obs], [proof], and [stop]. Blue arrows run from each journal row to the matching tag. The line under both cards says the file stays the source and the terminal reprints it. The arrows are the part that matters. Each tag is a reprint of the object just written to the file. If the file says allow, the tag says allow.

The live command prints the tool request as [tool?], question mark included, because that line is the ask before the gate answers. The picture shortens that row to a tool tag. Same row either way. You see the path and the content, and only then [gate] allow.

2144 chars

Why the reprint has to match

A terminal view is easy to let drift from the file. Standard output saying allow, while the JSONL says deny, would be two stories about one run. This projector prints the object the loop just appended, so the two surfaces stay the same story.

You can watch the run, and you can feed an old transcript through the same function later. Allow still owns the write. Done is still the bytes in hello.txt.

400 chars

What the tui command wires

The tui command builds FakeModel in ok mode, FixedGate baked to allow, and an EventProjector. The projector's onEvent method is handed to the loop as a callback, a function you give to other code so it can call you back. After each journal append, the loop calls that callback with the same object it just wrote.

The task line is: Create hello.txt containing exactly ok.

} else if (isTui) {
  const projector = new EventProjector();
  onEvent = projector.onEvent;
  model = new FakeModel("ok");
  gate = new FixedGate("allow");
}

The loop still journals, still records allow, still writes hello.txt, still reads the bytes. The extra work is the callback. Ordinary allow demos skip it. The tui command is the one that turns the projector on.

A successful run prints this shape. Paths on your machine are longer than the dots.

=== harness run ===
[task] Create hello.txt containing exactly ok
[model] step=1 tool → write_file
[tool?] step=1 write_file path=…/hello.txt content="ok"
[gate] step=1 allow
[obs] step=1 {"path":"…/hello.txt","content":"ok"}
[model] step=2 stop → hello.txt contains exactly ok
[proof] exactBytes=true expected=6f6b actual=6f6b
[stop] step=2 hello.txt contains exactly ok
=== done ===

6f6b is the byte for o, then the byte for k. exactBytes true means those bytes were what the harness read back from hello.txt.

Then the command prints the model answer and a line that names transcripts/tui.jsonl. The JSONL ends on stop, and the proof says exactBytes true.

[tool?] is the request before the gate answers. Request is recorded before Allow. Observation is recorded after the write. Proof is recorded after the harness reads the file itself.

Tests lock the tags on standard output and the file on disk. Status 0. The last JSONL event is stop. The approval result is allow. Standard output contains [task], [gate] with allow, [proof], [stop], and a transcript= line that names tui.jsonl.

1372 chars

One event, some lines

src/tui.ts keeps a pure function, projectEvent. One journal object in. Zero or more display lines out. No disk write. No network call. Color is optional, using the ANSI byte sequences a terminal understands. ANSI is the old standard that named those color codes. When standard output is not a terminal, or when a test sets useAnsi to false, the tags stay and the color bytes go away. A terminal attached to the stream is what Node calls a TTY, short for the old teletype.

export function projectEvent(event: JournalEvent, useAnsi = false): string[] {
  const tag = (label: string, color: string) => paint(useAnsi, color, `[${label}]`);
  const step = typeof event.step === "number" ? ` step=${event.step}` : "";

  switch (event.event) {
    case "user":
      return [
        paint(useAnsi, BOLD, "=== harness run ==="),
        `${tag("task", CYAN)} ${event.task ?? ""}`
      ];
    case "model_decision": {
      const d = event.decision;
      if (d?.kind === "stop") {
        return [`${tag("model", CYAN)}${step} stop → ${d.answer ?? ""}`];
      }
      if (d?.kind === "tool") {
        return [`${tag("model", CYAN)}${step} tool → ${d.tool ?? "?"}`];
      }
      return [`${tag("model", CYAN)}${step} ${JSON.stringify(d ?? {})}`];
    }
    // approval, observation, proof, stop follow the same tag pattern
  }
}

A unit test, a small automated check of one piece on its own, feeds a known sequence, task then write request then allow then observation then proof then stop, and asserts those tags. No color bytes in that capture. A remember line would render as [memory] if the journal had one. This demo stores no memory note. The run is the ordinary write, with the projector hooked up.

EventProjector holds the write sink, console.log unless you pass another, and the color flag, on when process.stdout is a TTY. onEvent is the live callback. projectAll walks an array of events and calls the same projectEvent. Live and replay stay together because there is one renderer in this file.

onEvent = (raw: object): void => {
  const event = raw as JournalEvent;
  for (const line of projectEvent(event, this.useAnsi)) {
    this.lines.push(line);
    this.write(line);
  }
};

Pipe npm run tui into a file and the tags remain. Color drops because standard output is not a terminal. Tests force useAnsi false and check that the joined lines contain no escape bytes.

1337 chars

Disk first, then the screen

The loop writes the journal in one helper. Append the line. Then notify.

async function event(
  path: string,
  value: object,
  onEvent?: (event: object) => void
): Promise<void> {
  await mkdir(dirname(path), { recursive: true });
  await appendFile(path, JSON.stringify(value) + "\n", "utf8");
  onEvent?.(value);
}

Order matters. Disk first. Screen second. If the append throws, you do not print a line that never landed. onEvent is optional. The callback does not change the proof. The harness still reads hello.txt and still demands the bytes ok.

A unit test runs the loop with onEvent pushing into an array, then reads the JSONL and checks the two lists match, object for object. Same count. The last event is stop.

The next picture is that order, with replay beside the live path.

The title is Live and replay. The top row is the live path. Journal append, with the note that events are appended to the journal, then the onEvent callback, which calls projectEvent for each new event, then tagged stdout. The bottom row starts from an existing JSONL file, read line by line, then projectAll, which calls projectEvent for each existing event, then the same tags. The caption says live and replay share projectEvent. An orange note says the renderer does not write hello.txt. A bar along the bottom says proof unchanged: the same input events lead to the same projectEvent calls and the same output. The orange note is the part that matters. Reprinting a log must not create the file, and must not ask Allow again.

Replay is the same function without a live guest. Load the lines. Call projectAll. You get the tags again, which is how you read transcripts/tui.jsonl as a person. Replay only prints. Tools stay idle, Allow is left unasked, and hello.txt stays as it was.

1533 chars

Honest limits

Color is optional, and it drops when standard output is not a terminal. Fullscreen chrome, mouse input, and split panes stay out of this command. So does a screen library. It adds no packages.

The projector leaves Allow and the proof alone. FakeModel still proposes the write. FixedGate still answers yes. The harness still writes hello.txt and still reads the bytes. A green tag is a reprint. The file is the proof.

417 chars

What to run

Clone the public repo if you do not have it. You need Node 22 or newer. The script turns on the flag that runs TypeScript (JavaScript with type annotations) without a separate compile step.

git clone https://github.com/ashishpatill/harness-from-scratch
cd harness-from-scratch
npm run tui

Open transcripts/tui.jsonl and hello.txt.

After that command, the terminal has printed the task, the allow, the proof, and the stop, and transcripts/tui.jsonl holds those same events in that order. hello.txt is the two letters ok. The proof line says the harness re-read the file and the bytes matched. The screen followed the log the harness had already written.
